title: When and What to Prune? Stage-Aware Visual Token Pruning for Efficient VLA

paper.title:
When and What to Prune?
Stage-Aware Visual Token Pruning for Efficient VLA
paper.abstract: Abstract Visual token pruning is an effective way to accelerate vision-language models and is especially useful for vision-language-action (VLA) inference, where many visual tokens must be processed before predicting robot actions. Existing pruning methods usually estimate which tokens can be pruned based on attention scores or feature diversity, retaining tokens that are either highly attended or visually different from others. However, most of them use fixed pruning schedules, such as pruning once at a preset layer or pruning at uniformly spaced layers. Such schedules can be risky for VLA models, because the model may not know which visual regions matter for the action in early layers. Tokens that look unimportant at first may become useful after the model combines visual observations with the language instruction. In this work, we propose SAPrune , a training-free visual token pruning framework for efficient VLA inference. Instead of pruning at fixed layers, SAPrune uses a small calibration set to observe how action-to-visual attention changes across layers, and chooses pruning layers only after the attention pattern becomes more reliable. At each selected layer, SAPrune applies a dual-path pruning rule: one path protects strongly attended visual tokens from pruning, while the other prevents useful surrounding context from being discarded. Experiments on LIBERO, SIMPLER, and real-world robotic tasks show that SAPrune prunes 87.5% of visual tokens and achieves up to 1.718 × \times inference speedup while maintaining competitive task success rates.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently shown strong potential for embodied decision making by mapping visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Despite their effectiveness, VLA inference remains computationally expensive because a large number of visual tokens must be propagated through deep Transformer layers [ 5 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Visual token pruning is therefore a natural direction for reducing latency and computation, as shown in prior studies on efficient Vision Transformers and large vision-language models [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . Figure 1 : Layer-wise visualization of attention in VLA. Although recent studies have shown substantial redundancy in VLA inference, most pruning-oriented acceleration methods still decide token removal from local importance cues, visual saliency, feature-space diversity, or their fixed combinations [ 13 , 15 , 14 , 16 , 18 , 17 , 8 , 9 ] . This treats pruning mainly as a static token-selection problem. Such a formulation is insufficient for action generation, where visual evidence does not remain fixed across depth: it gradually emerges, redistributes, and stabilizes as the model forms an action decision. Moreover, visual distinctiveness alone does not imply decision usefulness, since tokens that are geometrically diverse may still be irrelevant to the current action. These limitations motivate us to reconsider VLA pruning from two questions: when pruning becomes reliable, and what action-relevant evidence should be preserved. To understand when visual tokens can be safely pruned during VLA inference, we analyze the attention from action-related states to visual tokens across Transformer layers. Figure 1 shows that early layers attend to a broad set of visual tokens, while middle and deep layers gradually concentrate on tokens related to the target action. Figure 2(a) further quantifies this trend using the top- k k attention mass: the mass increases quickly from shallow to middle layers and then changes more slowly. This suggests that early layers have not yet clearly determined which visual tokens are useful for the action. Therefore, pruning too early may remove tokens that become important later, motivating us to delay pruning until the attention pattern becomes more stable. We further compare different pruning criteria in Fig. 2(b) . Attention-only selection tends to concentrate on dominant regions and may miss supportive context, whereas feature-space diversity-based selection may retain tokens that are visually distinctive but weakly related to the current action. These observations suggest that attention-only selection, feature-space diversity-based selection, and their fixed combination are all insufficient for aggressive VLA pruning. (a) Visualization of Top-k Importance Image Token Received Attention Ratio. (b) Comparison of Performance under Different Token Pruning Strategies. Figure 2 : Preliminary observations on top-k attention concentration and token pruning strategy comparison. Based on these principles, we propose SAPrune , a training-free visual token pruning framework for efficient VLA inference. SAPrune first selects pruning layers from rollout-level action-attention dynamics, and then applies a dual-path retention mechanism at each selected layer. The attention-core path preserves directly action-relevant tokens, while the functional-diversity path selects complementary tokens using query-conditioned functional signatures. Experiments on LIBERO [ 19 ] , SIMPLER [ 20 ] , and real-world robotic tasks show that SAPrune retains only 32 visual tokens, prunes 87.5% of the original visual tokens, and achieves up to 1.718 × \times speedup while maintaining competitive task success rates.

sections.heading: 2.1 Related Works
sections.text: Efficient inference for VLA models. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models extend large vision-language models by introducing an action modality, enabling robots to predict executable actions from visual observations and language instructions. Representative generalist robot policies include RT-1 [ 1 ] , RT-2 [ 2 ] , Open X-Embodiment / RT-X [ 3 ] , Octo [ 4 ] , OpenVLA [ 5 ] , π 0 \pi_{0} [ 6 ] . Although effective for general-purpose manipulation, these models repeatedly process dense visual tokens through deep Transformer layers, making inference costly for real-time robot deployment [ 7 , 8 , 21 , 22 , 9 ] . Visual token pruning for VLMs. Visual token pruning reduces visual redundancy by retaining a compact subset of informative visual tokens. Early efficient Vision Transformer methods, such as DynamicViT [ 10 ] , EViT [ 11 ] , and ToMe [ 12 ] , reduce computation through token sparsification or merging. For large vision-language models, attention-based methods such as FastV [ 13 ] , SparseVLM [ 15 ] , FoPru [ 23 ] , HiPrune [ 24 ] , LVPruning [ 16 ] , IVTP [ 14 ] , and ZSPA-Prune [ 25 ] rank tokens by prefill attention, text-to-vision attention, or prompt-conditioned relevance. Other methods preserve diversity or global representativeness [ 17 , 18 , 26 , 27 ] , while calibration or layer-adaptive methods determine pruning layers, ratios, or progressive schedules from calibration statistics or cross-layer information flow [ 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 ] . However, these methods are mainly designed for VLM understanding and do not explicitly model action-dependent visual evidence in VLA inference. Training-free acceleration for VLA models. Training-free VLA acceleration mainly follows temporal reuse, adaptive computation, and pruning-based acceleration. VLA-Cache [ 7 ] reuses visual features across adjacent timesteps, while VLA-ADP [ 22 ] dynamically reduces computation during manipulation. EfficientVLA [ 8 ] , SP-VLA [ 21 ] , SpecPrune-VLA [ 33 ] , and VLA-Pruner [ 9 ] reduce visual-token computation during VLA inference. These methods reveal substantial redundancy in VLA models, but often rely on fixed pruning locations, semantic relevance, temporal reuse, or additional acceleration modules. They leave underexplored how to choose pruning layers and preserve action-relevant evidence under aggressive token reduction.

sections.heading: 2.2 VLA Inference and Action-to-Visual Attention
sections.text: VLA inference. Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to executable robot actions. At rollout step t t , the model takes an image observation I t I_{t} and a language instruction x t x_{t} as input, and predicts an action a t a_{t} . For notational simplicity, we omit the timestep index in the following. The vision encoder produces N N visual tokens V ( 0 ) = { v 1 ( 0 ) , … , v N ( 0 ) } V^{(0)}=\{v^{(0)}_{1},\ldots,v^{(0)}_{N}\} , while the text encoder produces M M text tokens X ( 0 ) = { x 1 ( 0 ) , … , x M ( 0 ) } X^{(0)}=\{x^{(0)}_{1},\ldots,x^{(0)}_{M}\} . Depending on the backbone, action-related states can be implemented as action tokens, action placeholders, or action query states, denoted by Q a ( 0 ) Q^{(0)}_{a} , as in OpenVLA [ 5 ] , π 0 \pi_{0} [ 6 ] . The initial multimodal sequence is H ( 0 ) = V ( 0 ) ⊕ X ( 0 ) ⊕ Q a ( 0 ) , H^{(0)}=V^{(0)}\oplus X^{(0)}\oplus Q^{(0)}_{a}, (1) where ⊕ \oplus denotes sequence concatenation. sections.heading: 3.1 Overview
sections.text: Figure 3 gives an overview of SAPrune . SAPrune uses layer-wise action-to-visual attention statistics to decide where pruning is applied. It first selects pruning layers from rollout-level action-attention dynamics, and then applies a layer-local dual-path pruning rule. Figure 3 : Overview of the framework.

sections.heading: 3.2 Pruning-layer selection from action-attention dynamics
3.3 Layer-Local Dual-Path Pruning
sections.text: At each selected pruning layer l l , the module receives the current visual token set V ( l ) = { z i ( l ) } i = 1 N l V^{(l)}=\{z_{i}^{(l)}\}_{i=1}^{N_{l}} and keeps K l K_{l} tokens. Let q a ( l ) q_{a}^{(l)} denote the action query and X ( l ) = { x 1 ( l ) , … , x M ( l ) } X^{(l)}=\{x_{1}^{(l)},\ldots,x_{M}^{(l)}\} denote the text-token representations. A simple baseline is to keep the top- K l K_{l} tokens ranked by action attention. However, this rule often collapses the retained set onto a small highly attended region and may remove nearby objects, spatial anchors, or background cues needed for control. SAPrune therefore splits token retention into two paths. The attention path keeps the highest-attention tokens, while the coverage path selects additional candidates whose query-response patterns are not already represented by the retained set.

sections.heading: 4 Experiment
sections.text: We evaluate SAPrune on two simulation benchmarks, LIBERO [ 19 ] and SIMPLER [ 20 ] , as well as on four real-world manipulation tasks. We compare our method with several representative efficient inference baselines, including FastV [ 13 ] , DivPrune [ 17 ] , SP-VLA [ 21 ] , VLA-ADP [ 22 ] , and EfficientVLA [ 8 ] , and instantiate them on three VLA backbones: OpenVLA [ 5 ] , OpenVLA-OFT [ 34 ] , and π 0 \pi_{0} [ 6 ] . For real-world evaluation, we deploy the system on an AgileX Piper. All latency results are measured on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. Unless stated otherwise, latency is measured with PyTorch SDPA for both the full model and SAPrune, without model compilation. FlashAttention-2 results are reported in Appendix B.4.3 .

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Compared Methods. We compare SAPrune with representative token-pruning baselines for efficient VLA inference, including FastV [ 13 ] , DivPrune [ 17 ] , SP-VLA [ 21 ] , VLA-ADP [ 22 ] , and EfficientVLA [ 8 ] . These methods cover the major pruning paradigms relevant to our setting: FastV [ 13 ] performs attention-based top-token selection, DivPrune [ 17 ] preserves visually diverse tokens to reduce redundancy, SP-VLA [ 21 ] applies structured pruning tailored to VLA inference, VLA-ADP [ 22 ] adaptively adjusts token retention during inference, and EfficientVLA [ 8 ] combines token relevance with feature-space diversity in a progressive pruning framework. For the main comparison, we follow the reported or default token settings of these methods rather than enforcing a unified token budget for all baselines. Specifically, the original models use 256 visual tokens, while different baselines adopt their own retained-token settings; our method keeps only 32 final visual tokens. To eliminate the effect of unequal token budgets, we further provide controlled comparisons under the same 32-token setting. sections.heading: 4.2 Results on Simulation Environment
sections.text: Results on LIBERO. Table 1 reports the main results on LIBERO [ 19 ] . Across OpenVLA [ 5 ] , OpenVLA-OFT [ 34 ] , and π 0 \pi_{0} [ 6 ] , SAPrune maintains success rates close to the full-token models while using a much smaller visual-token budget. It also brings clear efficiency gains, achieving 1.608 × \times , 1.718 × \times , and 1.532 × \times speedups on the three backbones, respectively, with substantial FLOPs reduction. Compared with existing pruning baselines, SAPrune achieves higher average success under a more aggressive final pruning ratio, indicating that aggressive pruning can remain reliable when token reduction is applied at more stable action-attention stages. The main degradation appears on the Long suite, where long-horizon manipulation is more sensitive to accumulated execution errors and extreme token reduction. Figure 11 provides additional LIBERO visualizations that qualitatively support the observed robustness under high-ratio pruning. We also evaluate SAPrune on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 35 ] on LIBERO. The complete results are shown in Table 3 . SAPrune reaches 95.9% average success versus 96.6% for the full model, while reducing E2E latency from 91.47 ms to 59.68 ms with 32 visual tokens versus 256 for the full model. This result extends the evaluation to a newer VLA backbone. Results on SIMPLER. Table 2 reports the results on the visible tasks in SIMPLER [ 20 ] under a compact 32-token budget. Under this aggressive pruning setting, SAPrune maintains substantially stronger task performance than other pruning baselines on the OpenVLA [ 5 ] backbone. While attention-based, structured, adaptive, and feature-diversity-based baselines suffer clear success drops after reducing the visual tokens to 32, SAPrune remains comparatively stable across PickCoke, MoveNear, and Open/Close. These results further indicate that, under high-ratio token reduction, selecting pruning stages from action-attention dynamics and preserving complementary action-language evidence are critical for maintaining reliable manipulation performance.

sections.heading: 4.3 Results on Real-World Environment
sections.text: Table 4 reports the real-world manipulation results on AgileX Piper with the π 0 \pi_{0} [ 6 ] backbone. The results show that SAPrune achieves the lowest inference cost among pruned methods while maintaining competitive task success rates. Figure 12 provides qualitative rollouts on the AgileX Piper robot. We also measure end-to-end latency on the same real-robot runs. The complete comparison is shown in Table 9 . SAPrune reduces latency from 88.68 ms to 61.97 ms and raises the policy-pipeline frequency from 11.28 to 16.14 Hz, a 30.1% latency reduction. Physical actuation and low-level servo time are excluded.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We present SAPrune, a training-free visual token pruning framework for efficient VLA inference under aggressive token reduction. Instead of treating pruning as a static token-ranking problem, SAPrune addresses two practical questions for VLA deployment: when pruning should be applied, and which visual tokens can be safely removed. The proposed pruning-layer selection avoids arbitrary layer choices by using rollout-derived action-to-visual attention statistics to identify more reliable pruning stages. At each selected layer, the dual-path pruning rule removes redundant visual tokens while reducing the risk of pruning strongly attended action cues or useful surrounding context. This design requires no retraining or architectural modification, making SAPrune compatible with different VLA backbones.

sections.heading: B.1 VLA Model Details
sections.text: We evaluate SAPrune on representative VLA backbones, including OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, π 0 \pi_{0} , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . These models cover both autoregressive action-token policies and flow-based continuous-action policies, allowing us to examine whether the proposed pruning strategy generalizes across different action-generation mechanisms.

sections.heading: OpenVLA.
sections.text: OpenVLA [ 5 ] is a 7B open-source vision-language-action model adapted from a pretrained vision-language model for robotic control. It encodes visual observations and language instructions, and predicts discretized robot actions through autoregressive token generation. We use OpenVLA as the representative token-based VLA backbone.

sections.heading: OpenVLA-OFT.
sections.text: OpenVLA-OFT [ 34 ] is an optimized fine-tuning variant of OpenVLA. It improves the original action-generation recipe with parallel decoding, action chunking, continuous action representation, and regression-based training objectives. Compared with the original OpenVLA, it provides stronger control performance and higher inference efficiency while preserving the same general VLA formulation. We use OpenVLA-OFT as a stronger OpenVLA-family backbone.

sections.heading: π 0 \pi_{0} Model.
sections.text: π 0 \pi_{0} [ 6 ] is a flow-based vision-language-action model for general robot control. Instead of decoding discretized action tokens autoregressively, it augments a pretrained vision-language model with a continuous-action flow-matching module. This makes π 0 \pi_{0} representative of continuous-action VLA policies and complements the OpenVLA-family models in our evaluation.

sections.heading: π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} Model.
sections.text: π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 35 ] is a newer VLA model designed for open-world generalization. We evaluate it on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus using the same calibration and pruning procedure, without manual pruning-layer tuning.

sections.heading: B.2 Acceleration Baseline Details
sections.text: We compare SAPrune with representative training-free or plug-and-play acceleration baselines, including FastV, DivPrune, SP-VLA, VLA-ADP, and EfficientVLA. These methods cover attention-based pruning, diversity-based pruning, structured VLA pruning, adaptive pruning, and progressive VLA acceleration.

sections.heading: FastV.
sections.text: FastV [ 13 ] is a training-free attention-based pruning method for large vision-language models. It ranks visual tokens by attention-derived importance and removes low-score tokens after a selected layer. Since it relies mainly on attention relevance, we use it as an attention-only pruning baseline.

sections.heading: DivPrune.
sections.text: DivPrune [ 17 ] selects visual tokens by encouraging feature-space diversity among the retained set. It reduces redundancy by preserving visually dissimilar tokens, but its diversity criterion is not explicitly conditioned on action generation. We use it as a representative diversity-based pruning baseline.

sections.heading: SP-VLA.
sections.text: SP-VLA [ 21 ] is a VLA-oriented acceleration method that combines model scheduling with token pruning. Compared with generic VLM pruning methods, it is more tailored to VLA inference. We include it as a structured VLA pruning baseline.

sections.heading: VLA-ADP.
sections.text: VLA-ADP [ 22 ] performs action-aware dynamic pruning for efficient VLA manipulation. It adaptively adjusts token retention during inference rather than using a completely fixed pruning rule. We use it as a representative adaptive VLA pruning baseline.

sections.heading: EfficientVLA.
sections.text: EfficientVLA [ 8 ] is a recent training-free acceleration framework for VLA models. Its pruning component combines token relevance with feature-space diversity in a progressive pruning pipeline. We include EfficientVLA, especially its text-guided variant EfficientVLA(T-only), as a strong relevance-plus-diversity baseline.

sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: We report two groups of comparisons. In the default-budget setting, each baseline is evaluated under its reported or recommended token budget, while the original models use 256 visual tokens and SAPrune keeps 32 visual tokens. This setting reflects the practical configuration of each method. In the controlled-budget setting, we fix the final retained-token budget to 32 for all applicable pruning methods, so that performance differences mainly reflect the token-selection strategy rather than the number of remaining visual tokens. sections.heading: B.3 Benchmarks and Tasks
sections.text: We evaluate SAPrune on three groups of benchmarks: LIBERO [ 19 ] , SIMPLER [ 20 ] , and a set of real-world robotic manipulation tasks, as shown in Figure 6 . These benchmarks cover both simulation and real-robot settings, and include tasks with different horizons, scene complexity, and semantic requirements.

sections.heading: LIBERO.
sections.text: LIBERO [ 19 ] is a language-conditioned manipulation benchmark built on Robosuite. We follow the standard four-suite protocol and evaluate on Spatial , Object , Goal , and Long , with 10 tasks in each suite. Spatial focuses on spatial relations under varying object configurations. Object changes the target object while keeping the task template relatively fixed. Goal evaluates goal-conditioned manipulation with different final states. Long contains multi-stage long-horizon tasks and is more sensitive to accumulated execution errors.

sections.heading: SIMPLER.
sections.text: SIMPLER [ 20 ] is a simulation benchmark designed to better reflect real-robot manipulation performance. We evaluate on four Google-Robot-style tasks: Pick Coke , Move Near , Open Drawer , and Close Drawer . These tasks cover common short-horizon manipulation primitives, including grasping, local object repositioning, and articulated-object interaction. SIMPLER complements LIBERO by providing visually grounded tabletop tasks with a closer connection to real-robot evaluation.

sections.heading: Real-world tasks.
sections.text: We further conduct real-world experiments on an AgileX Piper robot. The real-world suite includes Cube Grasping , Pick&Place , Select-Pick&Place , and Multi-Cube Stacking . Cube Grasping evaluates basic target localization and grasp execution. Pick&Place tests object transport and placement. Select-Pick&Place introduces distractor objects and requires target selection before manipulation. Multi-Cube Stacking requires repeated grasping and placement, and is the most sequential task in this suite. These real-world tasks test whether aggressive visual-token pruning remains reliable under practical sensing and execution conditions.

sections.heading: B.4.1 Controlled Comparison Under a Unified 32-Token Budget
sections.text: Table 6 compares all applicable pruning methods on LIBERO under the same final budget of 32 visual tokens. SAPrune consistently achieves the strongest task performance across OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and π 0 \pi_{0} , indicating that its advantage comes from stage-aware pruning-layer placement and higher-quality token retention rather than from using more final tokens. SAPrune can be slightly slower than some baselines because it delays pruning until more reliable stages and reduces visual tokens progressively across selected layers, so earlier layers still process more tokens than early one-step pruning methods. Nevertheless, it preserves substantially higher success rates while still accelerating the full-token model, yielding the best overall efficiency-performance balance under the same token budget. sections.heading: Appendix C Limitation
sections.text: SAPrune is built on the empirically supported premise that action-to-visual attention can serve as a useful proxy for action-relevant visual evidence. Our experiments suggest that this premise holds well for sufficiently trained VLA backbones whose action-related states are grounded in task-relevant visual regions. Under such conditions, SAPrune is better aligned with VLA inference than generic visual-token pruning methods because it delays pruning until action-conditioned attention becomes stable and preserves both dominant and complementary visual evidence. However, this premise may become weaker when the backbone attention is poorly grounded, remains diffuse, or is dominated by spurious background regions. In such cases, the attention signal may not accurately reflect the causal contribution of visual tokens, and SAPrune may still introduce performance degradation, especially in scenarios involving out-of-distribution objects, fine-grained contact regions, heavy occlusion, or long-horizon manipulation. SAPrune also requires visual and action-related representations to interact within the Transformer being pruned. This holds for the implementations evaluated here. In separated vision-language model (VLM) and diffusion Transformer (DiT) systems, action-conditioned queries may be available only in the downstream action module. Direct use in the VLM then requires an adaptation across modules, which we have not evaluated. Pruning the VLM conditioning sequence would not remove the remaining DiT denoising computation, limiting the possible end-to-end speedup.

sections.heading: Appendix D Impact Statement
sections.text: This work aims to improve the efficiency of vision-language-action models by reducing visual-token computation during inference. More efficient VLA inference can lower latency and deployment cost, potentially making robotic manipulation systems more practical on resource-constrained hardware. At the same time, efficiency improvements may also make robotic automation easier to deploy at larger scale, which raises broader concerns about safety, accountability, and labor displacement. Since token pruning may remove visual evidence needed for reliable control in rare or out-of-distribution situations, SAPrune should be used with appropriate validation, monitoring, and task-specific safety constraints before real-world deployment.
